title: Pronoun case: I or me, who or whom
note: Use subject forms (I, he, she, we, they, who) for subjects and object forms (me, him, her, us, them, whom) for objects of verbs and prepositions. To check a pair, drop the other person: 'between you and me' is right because you would say 'between me'. For who or whom, answer the clause with he (who) or him (whom).

read.title: The drop-the-other-name test
text: Pronoun case means choosing the right form for a pronoun's job. Subjects take subject forms: I, he, she, we, they, who. Objects of verbs and prepositions take object forms: me, him, her, us, them, whom.

Few people say "Me went home" or "She called I." The errors appear when a pronoun is paired with another noun. "My brother and me fixed the sink" sounds acceptable to many ears, and "between you and I" can sound formal. A simple test exposes both. Remove the other person and read what is left: "Me fixed the sink" is plainly wrong, so the subject must be "My brother and I." "Between I" is wrong too, so the phrase is "between you and me."

Who and whom follow the same logic. Who is a subject, whom is an object. Isolate the clause and answer it with he or him. In "the student ___ we chose," the clause becomes "we chose him," so the word is whom. In "the student ___ won," it becomes "he won," so the word is who.
Nervous writers sometimes dodge the choice with myself, as in "Send it to Dana or myself." That is not more correct; it simply avoids the question. Use me.

q.q: How does the reading suggest checking "My brother and me fixed the sink"?
o: Read it with the other person removed

q.q: In "the student ___ we chose," which word fits and why?
o: who, because student is a subject
who, because it follows a noun

q.q: What does the reading say about "Send it to Dana or myself"?
o: It is the most formal choice
It is correct in business writing
It dodges the choice; use me
